import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Convex uniform 5-polytopes

A *convex uniform polytope* is defined recursively on the dimension. A uniform $0$-polytope is a
point. A uniform $d$-polytope ($d \ge 1$) is a convex $d$-polytope that is vertex-transitive (the
isometries of the ambient space mapping it onto itself act transitively on its vertices), whose
edges all have the same length, and whose facets are uniform $(d-1)$-polytopes. In dimension $2$
this gives the regular polygons and in dimension $3$ the convex uniform polyhedra (Platonic and
Archimedean solids, prisms and antiprisms). For $d \ge 3$ the condition on the edges is implied by
the other two conditions.

The complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes has not been determined. The known ones are:
* the Wythoffian polytopes of the irreducible reflection groups $A_5$ ($19$ polytopes),
  $B_5$ ($31$) and $D_5$ ($8$ not already in the $B_5$ family). A Wythoffian polytope is the
  convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection group;
* the prisms over the convex uniform 4-polytopes: the $45$ polychoral prisms not already counted
  (the prism over the tesseract is the 5-cube), the grand antiprism prism (the only known
  non-Wythoffian convex uniform 5-polytope), and the infinite family of duoprism prisms
  $\{p\}\times\{q\}\times\{\,\}$;
* the infinite duoprismatic families $\{q,r\}\times\{p\}$: Cartesian products of a convex uniform
  polyhedron and a regular polygon.

This gives $19 + 31 + 8 + 45 + 1 = 104$ known convex uniform 5-polytopes outside the infinite
families. The problem asks to find and classify the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes.

We formalise the statement that the known list is complete: every convex uniform 5-polytope in
$\mathbb{R}^5$ is Wythoffian, or a prism over a convex uniform 4-polytope, or the Cartesian
product of a convex uniform polyhedron and a regular polygon. Products are taken over all convex
uniform polytopes of the given dimensions (so, for instance, products of antiprisms or snub
polyhedra with regular polygons are included). Each of these three classes is closed under
similarities, so this is a statement about convex uniform 5-polytopes up to similarity. We also
record the literal open-ended form of the problem with `answer(sorry)`.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Uniform 5-polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/uniform_5-polytope)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Open Problem Garden, Convex uniform 5-polytopes](http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/convex_uniform_5_polytopes)
-/
open scoped EuclideanGeometry Pointwise
namespace Uniform5Polytope
variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]

blocks.code: def IsPolytope (P : Set E) : Prop := ∃ s : Finset E, P = convexHull ℝ (s : Set E)
blocks.docstring: A (convex) polytope in `E`: the convex hull of a finite set of points.

justification.closest_existing_considered: convexHull ℝ of a Finset (used in the definition); Mathlib only has lemmas like Set.Finite.isCompact_convexHull, no predicate.
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsPolytope
justification.why_needed: Mathlib has no notion of a convex polytope; needed as the convex hull of a finite set.

blocks.name: IsPolytope
blocks.text:
/-- A (convex) polytope in `E`: the convex hull of a finite set of points. -/
def IsPolytope (P : Set E) : Prop := ∃ s : Finset E, P = convexHull ℝ (s : Set E)

blocks.code: noncomputable def affDim (P : Set E) : ℕ := Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ P)
blocks.docstring: The affine dimension of a set `P`, i.e. the dimension of its affine span.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ s) (used inline in Mathlib, e.g. finrank_vectorSpan_of_affineIndependent, but not named).
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.affDim
justification.why_needed: Affine dimension of a set, to specify dimensions of polytopes and faces.

blocks.name: affDim
blocks.text:
/-- The affine dimension of a set `P`, i.e. the dimension of its affine span. -/
noncomputable def affDim (P : Set E) : ℕ := Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ P)

blocks.code: def IsFace (P F : Set E) (k : ℕ) : Prop := F.Nonempty ∧ IsExposed ℝ P F ∧ affDim F = k
blocks.docstring:
`F` is a `k`-dimensional face of the polytope `P`: a nonempty exposed subset of `P` (the set of
maximisers over `P` of a linear functional) of affine dimension `k`. All faces of a polytope are
exposed, so this captures all vertices (`k = 0`), edges (`k = 1`) and facets
(`k = affDim P - 1`).

justification.closest_existing_considered: IsExposed ℝ P F (used); Mathlib has no face-with-dimension notion or face lattice for polytopes.
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsFace
justification.why_needed: k-dimensional faces (edges, facets) of a polytope.

blocks.name: IsFace
blocks.text:
/-- `F` is a `k`-dimensional face of the polytope `P`: a nonempty exposed subset of `P` (the set of
maximisers over `P` of a linear functional) of affine dimension `k`. All faces of a polytope are
exposed, so this captures all vertices (`k = 0`), edges (`k = 1`) and facets
(`k = affDim P - 1`). -/
def IsFace (P F : Set E) (k : ℕ) : Prop := F.Nonempty ∧ IsExposed ℝ P F ∧ affDim F = k

blocks.code:
def IsVertexTransitive (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∀ v ∈ P.extremePoints ℝ, ∀ w ∈ P.extremePoints ℝ, ∃ g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E, g '' P = P ∧ g v = w
blocks.docstring:
`P` is vertex-transitive: for any two vertices (extreme points) `v`, `w` of `P` there is an
isometry `g` of `E` with `g '' P = P` and `g v = w`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: MulAction.IsPretransitive would need a stabilizer subgroup of E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E acting on extreme points; there is no MulAction (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) E instance, so a direct ∃-isometry formulation was used.
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsVertexTransitive
justification.why_needed: Vertex-transitivity of a polytope under Euclidean isometries.

blocks.name: IsVertexTransitive
blocks.text:
/-- `P` is vertex-transitive: for any two vertices (extreme points) `v`, `w` of `P` there is an
isometry `g` of `E` with `g '' P = P` and `g v = w`. -/
def IsVertexTransitive (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∀ v ∈ P.extremePoints ℝ, ∀ w ∈ P.extremePoints ℝ, ∃ g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E, g '' P = P ∧ g v = w

blocks.code:
def HasEqualEdges (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∀ e₁ e₂, IsFace P e₁ 1 → IsFace P e₂ 1 → Metric.diam e₁ = Metric.diam e₂
blocks.docstring: All edges (one-dimensional faces) of `P` have the same length.

justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.HasEqualEdges
justification.why_needed: All edges have the same length (part of the decomposition's definition of uniform).

blocks.name: HasEqualEdges

blocks.code:
def IsUniformPolytope : ℕ → Set E → Prop
  | 0, P => ∃ x, P = {x}
  | d + 1, P => IsPolytope P ∧ affDim P = d + 1 ∧ IsVertexTransitive P ∧ HasEqualEdges P ∧
      ∀ F, IsFace P F d → IsUniformPolytope d F
blocks.docstring:
`P` is a convex uniform `d`-polytope. A uniform `0`-polytope is a point. For `d ≥ 1`, a uniform
`d`-polytope is a `d`-dimensional polytope that is vertex-transitive, has all edges of the same
length, and all of whose facets are uniform `(d - 1)`-polytopes.

For `d = 1` this gives segments and for `d = 2` exactly the regular polygons, so for `d ≥ 3` this
is the usual recursive definition of a uniform polytope: vertex-transitive with uniform facets
(the condition on edges is then automatic). The symmetries of a lower-dimensional polytope are
taken to be the isometries of `E` mapping it onto itself; since every isometry of its affine span
extends to an isometry of `E`, this agrees with the intrinsic notion.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Nothing in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib (no polytopes, no regular polygons).
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsUniformPolytope
justification.why_needed: Recursive definition of convex uniform d-polytopes (regular polygons in dimension 2, vertex-transitive with uniform facets above).

blocks.name: IsUniformPolytope
blocks.text:
/-- `P` is a convex uniform `d`-polytope. A uniform `0`-polytope is a point. For `d ≥ 1`, a uniform
`d`-polytope is a `d`-dimensional polytope that is vertex-transitive, has all edges of the same
length, and all of whose facets are uniform `(d - 1)`-polytopes.

For `d = 1` this gives segments and for `d = 2` exactly the regular polygons, so for `d ≥ 3` this
is the usual recursive definition of a uniform polytope: vertex-transitive with uniform facets
(the condition on edges is then automatic). The symmetries of a lower-dimensional polytope are
taken to be the isometries of `E` mapping it onto itself; since every isometry of its affine span
extends to an isometry of `E`, this agrees with the intrinsic notion. -/
def IsUniformPolytope : ℕ → Set E → Prop
  | 0, P => ∃ x, P = {x}
  | d + 1, P => IsPolytope P ∧ affDim P = d + 1 ∧ IsVertexTransitive P ∧ HasEqualEdges P ∧
      ∀ F, IsFace P F d → IsUniformPolytope d F

theorem IsUniformPolytope.isPolytope_and_affDim {d : ℕ} {P : Set E}

blocks.docstring: A convex uniform `(d + 1)`-polytope is a polytope of dimension `d + 1`.
blocks.name: IsUniformPolytope.isPolytope_and_affDim
blocks.text:

variable [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]

blocks.docstring: `g` is the reflection of `E` in an affine hyperplane `H`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: EuclideanGeometry.reflection (used); Submodule.reflection (linear only, would need explicit translations); CoxeterSystem.IsReflection is for abstract Coxeter groups.
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsHyperplaneReflection
justification.why_needed: Predicate 'g is a reflection in an affine hyperplane' on affine isometries, to define reflection groups.

blocks.name: IsHyperplaneReflection
blocks.text:
/-- `g` is the reflection of `E` in an affine hyperplane `H`. -/
def IsHyperplaneReflection (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (H : AffineSubspace ℝ E) (_ : Nonempty H),
    Module.finrank ℝ H.direction + 1 = Module.finrank ℝ E ∧ g = EuclideanGeometry.reflection H

blocks.code:
def IsFiniteReflectionGroup (G : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) : Prop :=
  Finite G ∧ ∃ S : Set (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E), (∀ g ∈ S, IsHyperplaneReflection g) ∧ G = Subgroup.closure S
blocks.docstring:
`G` is a finite reflection group: a finite group of isometries of `E` generated by reflections
in hyperplanes.

justification.closest_existing_considered: CoxeterSystem / CoxeterMatrix and RootPairing.weylGroup: abstract or root-system based, no geometric 'finite reflection group of a Euclidean space' predicate.
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsFiniteReflectionGroup
justification.why_needed: Finite groups of isometries generated by hyperplane reflections (Coxeter groups acting on ℝ^5).

blocks.name: IsFiniteReflectionGroup
blocks.text:
/-- `G` is a finite reflection group: a finite group of isometries of `E` generated by reflections
in hyperplanes. -/
def IsFiniteReflectionGroup (G : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) : Prop :=
  Finite G ∧ ∃ S : Set (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E), (∀ g ∈ S, IsHyperplaneReflection g) ∧ G = Subgroup.closure S

blocks.docstring:
`P` is Wythoffian: it is the convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection
group (Wythoff's construction). The uniform polytopes of this form are exactly those obtained
from a ringed Coxeter diagram of a finite Coxeter group.

justification.closest_existing_considered: MulAction.orbit (no MulAction instance for AffineIsometryEquiv on E; used Set.range over the subgroup instead).
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsWythoffian
justification.why_needed: Wythoff's construction: convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection group.

blocks.name: IsWythoffian
blocks.text:
/-- `P` is Wythoffian: it is the convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection
group (Wythoff's construction). The uniform polytopes of this form are exactly those obtained
from a ringed Coxeter diagram of a finite Coxeter group. -/
def IsWythoffian (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (G : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) (x : E), IsFiniteReflectionGroup G ∧
    P = convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun g : G => (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) x)

blocks.docstring:
`P` is the Cartesian product of a convex uniform `m`-polytope `A` and a convex uniform
`n`-polytope `B` lying in orthogonal subspaces, realised as the Minkowski sum `A + B` with
`A ⊆ U` and `B ⊆ Uᗮ`. The case `n = 1` is a (right) prism over `A`; the case `(m, n) = (3, 2)`
is a polyhedron-polygon duoprism.

justification.closest_existing_considered: Set.prod inside WithLp 2 (E × F) would need an isometry to ℝ^5; the Minkowski sum A + B with A ⊆ U, B ⊆ Uᗮ (Pointwise set addition, Submodule.orthogonal) is equivalent and simpler.
justification.name: Uniform5Polytope.IsProductOfUniformPolytopes
justification.why_needed: Orthogonal Cartesian products (prisms, duoprisms) of uniform polytopes inside ℝ^5.

blocks.name: IsProductOfUniformPolytopes
blocks.text:
/-- `P` is the Cartesian product of a convex uniform `m`-polytope `A` and a convex uniform
`n`-polytope `B` lying in orthogonal subspaces, realised as the Minkowski sum `A + B` with
`A ⊆ U` and `B ⊆ Uᗮ`. The case `n = 1` is a (right) prism over `A`; the case `(m, n) = (3, 2)`
is a polyhedron-polygon duoprism. -/
def IsProductOfUniformPolytopes (m n : ℕ) (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (U : Submodule ℝ E) (A B : Set E), A ⊆ U ∧ B ⊆ Uᗮ ∧
    IsUniformPolytope m A ∧ IsUniformPolytope n B ∧ P = A + B

blocks.code:
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem isWythoffian_singleton (x : E) : IsWythoffian ({x} : Set E) := by
  refine ⟨⊥, x, ⟨inferInstance, ∅, by simp, Subgroup.closure_empty.symm⟩, ?_⟩
  have : Set.range (fun g : (⊥ : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) => (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) x) = {x} := by
    ext y
    simp only [Set.mem_range, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    exact ⟨fun ⟨g, hg⟩ => by rw [← hg, show (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) = 1 from Subgroup.mem_bot.mp g.2]; rfl,
      fun h => ⟨1, by rw [h]; rfl⟩⟩
  rw [this, convexHull_singleton]
blocks.docstring: A point is Wythoffian (take the trivial reflection group).
blocks.name: isWythoffian_singleton
blocks.text:
/-- A point is Wythoffian (take the trivial reflection group). -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem isWythoffian_singleton (x : E) : IsWythoffian ({x} : Set E) := by
  refine ⟨⊥, x, ⟨inferInstance, ∅, by simp, Subgroup.closure_empty.symm⟩, ?_⟩
  have : Set.range (fun g : (⊥ : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) => (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) x) = {x} := by
    ext y
    simp only [Set.mem_range, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    exact ⟨fun ⟨g, hg⟩ => by rw [← hg, show (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) = 1 from Subgroup.mem_bot.mp g.2]; rfl,
      fun h => ⟨1, by rw [h]; rfl⟩⟩
  rw [this, convexHull_singleton]

@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem uniform_5_polytope (P : Set (ℝ^5)) (hP : IsUniformPolytope 5 P) :
    IsWythoffian P ∨ IsProductOfUniformPolytopes 4 1 P ∨ IsProductOfUniformPolytopes 3 2 P := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Convex uniform 5-polytopes**: find and classify the complete set of these shapes.

We state the conjecture that the known list is complete: every convex uniform 5-polytope is
* a Wythoffian polytope, i.e. the convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection
  group (the $19 + 31 + 8 = 58$ non-prismatic polytopes of the $A_5$, $B_5$ and $D_5$ families;
  reducible reflection groups only give prisms and duoprisms, which fall under the next two
  cases), or
* a prism over a convex uniform 4-polytope (the $45$ polychoral prisms, the grand antiprism prism
  and the duoprism prisms $\{p\}\times\{q\}\times\{\,\}$), or
* the Cartesian product of a convex uniform polyhedron and a regular polygon (the duoprismatic
  families $\{q,r\}\times\{p\}$).

Each of the three cases is invariant under similarities, so the statement classifies convex
uniform 5-polytopes up to similarity. It says that the list of $104$ known convex uniform
5-polytopes, together with the infinite prismatic families, is complete.

claims.decomposer_note: Open-ended classification, but the article asserts a candidate answer (104 known sporadic convex uniform 5-polytopes — 19 A5, 31 B5, 8 D5-unique, 45 unique polychoral prisms, and the non-Wythoffian grand antiprism prism — plus the infinite duoprism-prism {p}×{q}×{ } and uniform-polyhedron–polygon duoprism families), so the Prop is 'every convex uniform 5-polytope is, up to similarity, one of these'; subtleties are the recursive definition of uniform (vertex-transitive, all edges equal, facets uniform 4-polytopes), counting up to similarity/geometric identity rather than by Coxeter-diagram construction (e.g. B5/D5 duplicates, {4}×{4}×{ } = 5-cube), and the exact membership of the infinite families.
claims.reviewer_why: c03's file (used with light edits: extra API lemma, expanded module/theorem docstrings) states the decomposition's Prop faithfully: every convex uniform 5-polytope in R^5 (recursive definition: finite convex hull of the right affine dimension, vertex-transitive under ambient affine isometries, equal edges, facets uniform; base case a point) is a reflective Wythoffian orbit polytope, or an orthogonal product of uniform 4- and 1-polytopes (prisms over uniform 4-polytopes: the 45 polychoral prisms, grand antiprism prism, 5-cube, duoprism prisms), or an orthogonal product of a uniform polyhedron and a regular polygon. I verified this is equivalent to 'the known list is complete': 5-dimensional uniform orbit polytopes come from essential rank-5 reflection groups, whose irreducible ones are exactly A5/B5/D5 (ringed Wythoffians; B5/D5 geometric duplicates are handled automatically since we quantify over geometric subsets), and reducible ones give products; the (1,4)/(2,3) products coincide with (4,1)/(3,2) by symmetry of A ⊆ U, B ⊆ Uᗮ. Each disjunct is similarity-invariant so 'up to similarity' is handled. c02 and c06 state the same content (c02 with explicit congruence and k ranging over 1..4; c06 with redundant edge-matching) and would also have been acceptable; c03 was preferred for its cleaner affine reflection-group definition (absorbing translations) and product definition. c03's answer(sorry) variant `{P | IsUniformPolytope 5 P} = answer(sorry)` is kept as the literal 'find the complete set' form (the pattern CONTRIBUTING endorses). c05 gave only an answer(sorry) form (faithful but does not state the decomposition's Prop). The bail-outs (c01, c04, c07, c08) claimed 104 explicit coordinate models were required; the structural description is mathematically equivalent and avoids that, so their omission reasons were not compelling.

context:
In geometry, a uniform 5-polytope is a five-dimensional uniform polytope. By definition, a uniform 5-polytope is vertex-transitive and constructed from uniform 4-polytope facets.
The complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes has not been determined, but many can be made as Wythoff constructions from a small set of symmetry groups. These construction operations are represented by the permutations of rings of the Coxeter diagrams.

decomposition_objections.text: The table calls the article's 104 known polytopes plus infinite families a 'candidate answer' and fixes the Prop as 'every convex uniform 5-polytope is, up to similarity, one of these'. The article itself only says these are the known ones ('the complete set ... has not been determined'), and the list entry asks to 'find and classify', i.e. a determination problem. I conformed to the table's Prop, but (i) the list is rendered structurally (Wythoffian ∪ prisms over uniform 4-polytopes ∪ polyhedron × polygon) because a literal enumeration of 104 coordinate sets would be unverifiable and the table itself flags that the exact membership of the infinite families is unclear; in particular antiprism × polygon and prisms over antiprismatic prisms are convex uniform 5-polytopes that the article's family descriptions only include implicitly via alternations, so the structural reading is the one under which the completeness statement is not trivially false; (ii) I added the literal open-ended form as the variant `uniform_5_polytope.variants.find` with `answer(sorry)`.

A *convex uniform polytope* is defined recursively on the dimension. A uniform $0$-polytope is a
point. A uniform $d$-polytope ($d \ge 1$) is a convex $d$-polytope that is vertex-transitive (the
isometries of the ambient space mapping it onto itself act transitively on its vertices), whose
edges all have the same length, and whose facets are uniform $(d-1)$-polytopes. In dimension $2$
this gives the regular polygons and in dimension $3$ the convex uniform polyhedra (Platonic and
Archimedean solids, prisms and antiprisms). For $d \ge 3$ the condition on the edges is implied by
the other two conditions.

The complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes has not been determined. The known ones are:
* the Wythoffian polytopes of the irreducible reflection groups $A_5$ ($19$ polytopes),
  $B_5$ ($31$) and $D_5$ ($8$ not already in the $B_5$ family). A Wythoffian polytope is the
  convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection group;
* the prisms over the convex uniform 4-polytopes: the $45$ polychoral prisms not already counted
  (the prism over the tesseract is the 5-cube), the grand antiprism prism (the only known
  non-Wythoffian convex uniform 5-polytope), and the infinite family of duoprism prisms
  $\{p\}\times\{q\}\times\{\,\}$;
* the infinite duoprismatic families $\{q,r\}\times\{p\}$: Cartesian products of a convex uniform
  polyhedron and a regular polygon.

This gives $19 + 31 + 8 + 45 + 1 = 104$ known convex uniform 5-polytopes outside the infinite
families. The problem asks to find and classify the complete set of convex uniform 5-polytopes.

We formalise the statement that the known list is complete: every convex uniform 5-polytope in
$\mathbb{R}^5$ is Wythoffian, or a prism over a convex uniform 4-polytope, or the Cartesian
product of a convex uniform polyhedron and a regular polygon. Products are taken over all convex
uniform polytopes of the given dimensions (so, for instance, products of antiprisms or snub
polyhedra with regular polygons are included). Each of these three classes is closed under
similarities, so this is a statement about convex uniform 5-polytopes up to similarity. We also
record the literal open-ended form of the problem with `answer(sorry)`.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Uniform 5-polytope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/uniform_5-polytope)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Open Problem Garden, Convex uniform 5-polytopes](http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/convex_uniform_5_polytopes)
-/

open scoped EuclideanGeometry Pointwise

namespace Uniform5Polytope

variable {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E]

/-- A (convex) polytope in `E`: the convex hull of a finite set of points. -/
def IsPolytope (P : Set E) : Prop := ∃ s : Finset E, P = convexHull ℝ (s : Set E)

/-- The affine dimension of a set `P`, i.e. the dimension of its affine span. -/
noncomputable def affDim (P : Set E) : ℕ := Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ P)

/-- `F` is a `k`-dimensional face of the polytope `P`: a nonempty exposed subset of `P` (the set of
maximisers over `P` of a linear functional) of affine dimension `k`. All faces of a polytope are
exposed, so this captures all vertices (`k = 0`), edges (`k = 1`) and facets
(`k = affDim P - 1`). -/
def IsFace (P F : Set E) (k : ℕ) : Prop := F.Nonempty ∧ IsExposed ℝ P F ∧ affDim F = k

/-- `P` is vertex-transitive: for any two vertices (extreme points) `v`, `w` of `P` there is an
isometry `g` of `E` with `g '' P = P` and `g v = w`. -/
def IsVertexTransitive (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∀ v ∈ P.extremePoints ℝ, ∀ w ∈ P.extremePoints ℝ, ∃ g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E, g '' P = P ∧ g v = w

/-- All edges (one-dimensional faces) of `P` have the same length. -/
def HasEqualEdges (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∀ e₁ e₂, IsFace P e₁ 1 → IsFace P e₂ 1 → Metric.diam e₁ = Metric.diam e₂

/-- `P` is a convex uniform `d`-polytope. A uniform `0`-polytope is a point. For `d ≥ 1`, a uniform
`d`-polytope is a `d`-dimensional polytope that is vertex-transitive, has all edges of the same
length, and all of whose facets are uniform `(d - 1)`-polytopes.

For `d = 1` this gives segments and for `d = 2` exactly the regular polygons, so for `d ≥ 3` this
is the usual recursive definition of a uniform polytope: vertex-transitive with uniform facets
(the condition on edges is then automatic). The symmetries of a lower-dimensional polytope are
taken to be the isometries of `E` mapping it onto itself; since every isometry of its affine span
extends to an isometry of `E`, this agrees with the intrinsic notion. -/
def IsUniformPolytope : ℕ → Set E → Prop
  | 0, P => ∃ x, P = {x}
  | d + 1, P => IsPolytope P ∧ affDim P = d + 1 ∧ IsVertexTransitive P ∧ HasEqualEdges P ∧
      ∀ F, IsFace P F d → IsUniformPolytope d F

/-- A point is a uniform `0`-polytope. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem isUniformPolytope_zero_singleton (x : E) : IsUniformPolytope 0 ({x} : Set E) := ⟨x, rfl⟩

/-- A convex uniform `(d + 1)`-polytope is a polytope of dimension `d + 1`. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem IsUniformPolytope.isPolytope_and_affDim {d : ℕ} {P : Set E}
    (hP : IsUniformPolytope (d + 1) P) : IsPolytope P ∧ affDim P = d + 1 :=
  ⟨hP.1, hP.2.1⟩

variable [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]

/-- `g` is the reflection of `E` in an affine hyperplane `H`. -/
def IsHyperplaneReflection (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (H : AffineSubspace ℝ E) (_ : Nonempty H),
    Module.finrank ℝ H.direction + 1 = Module.finrank ℝ E ∧ g = EuclideanGeometry.reflection H

/-- `G` is a finite reflection group: a finite group of isometries of `E` generated by reflections
in hyperplanes. -/
def IsFiniteReflectionGroup (G : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) : Prop :=
  Finite G ∧ ∃ S : Set (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E), (∀ g ∈ S, IsHyperplaneReflection g) ∧ G = Subgroup.closure S

/-- `P` is Wythoffian: it is the convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection
group (Wythoff's construction). The uniform polytopes of this form are exactly those obtained
from a ringed Coxeter diagram of a finite Coxeter group. -/
def IsWythoffian (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (G : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) (x : E), IsFiniteReflectionGroup G ∧
    P = convexHull ℝ (Set.range fun g : G => (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) x)

/-- `P` is the Cartesian product of a convex uniform `m`-polytope `A` and a convex uniform
`n`-polytope `B` lying in orthogonal subspaces, realised as the Minkowski sum `A + B` with
`A ⊆ U` and `B ⊆ Uᗮ`. The case `n = 1` is a (right) prism over `A`; the case `(m, n) = (3, 2)`
is a polyhedron-polygon duoprism. -/
def IsProductOfUniformPolytopes (m n : ℕ) (P : Set E) : Prop :=
  ∃ (U : Submodule ℝ E) (A B : Set E), A ⊆ U ∧ B ⊆ Uᗮ ∧
    IsUniformPolytope m A ∧ IsUniformPolytope n B ∧ P = A + B

/-- A point is Wythoffian (take the trivial reflection group). -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem isWythoffian_singleton (x : E) : IsWythoffian ({x} : Set E) := by
  refine ⟨⊥, x, ⟨inferInstance, ∅, by simp, Subgroup.closure_empty.symm⟩, ?_⟩
  have : Set.range (fun g : (⊥ : Subgroup (E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E)) => (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) x) = {x} := by
    ext y
    simp only [Set.mem_range, Set.mem_singleton_iff]
    exact ⟨fun ⟨g, hg⟩ => by rw [← hg, show (g : E ≃ᵃⁱ[ℝ] E) = 1 from Subgroup.mem_bot.mp g.2]; rfl,
      fun h => ⟨1, by rw [h]; rfl⟩⟩
  rw [this, convexHull_singleton]

/--
**Convex uniform 5-polytopes**: find and classify the complete set of these shapes.

We state the conjecture that the known list is complete: every convex uniform 5-polytope is
* a Wythoffian polytope, i.e. the convex hull of the orbit of a point under a finite reflection
  group (the $19 + 31 + 8 = 58$ non-prismatic polytopes of the $A_5$, $B_5$ and $D_5$ families;
  reducible reflection groups only give prisms and duoprisms, which fall under the next two
  cases), or
* a prism over a convex uniform 4-polytope (the $45$ polychoral prisms, the grand antiprism prism
  and the duoprism prisms $\{p\}\times\{q\}\times\{\,\}$), or
* the Cartesian product of a convex uniform polyhedron and a regular polygon (the duoprismatic
  families $\{q,r\}\times\{p\}$).

Each of the three cases is invariant under similarities, so the statement classifies convex
uniform 5-polytopes up to similarity. It says that the list of $104$ known convex uniform
5-polytopes, together with the infinite prismatic families, is complete.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem uniform_5_polytope (P : Set (ℝ^5)) (hP : IsUniformPolytope 5 P) :
    IsWythoffian P ∨ IsProductOfUniformPolytopes 4 1 P ∨ IsProductOfUniformPolytopes 3 2 P := by
  sorry

/-- The problem in its original open-ended form: find the complete set of convex uniform
5-polytopes, as subsets of $\mathbb{R}^5$. This set is closed under similarities, so determining
it is the same as classifying convex uniform 5-polytopes up to similarity. -/
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem uniform_5_polytope.variants.find :
    {P : Set (ℝ^5) | IsUniformPolytope 5 P} = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

end Uniform5Polytope

items: The slot Prop follows the decomposition table ('every convex uniform 5-polytope is one of the known ones'), but the known list is described structurally as three similarity-invariant classes (reflective Wythoffian; prism over a convex uniform 4-polytope; convex uniform polyhedron × regular polygon) instead of enumerating 104 coordinate sets plus families. Set-theoretically this equals the article's list: the irreducible rank-5 reflection groups are exactly A5, B5, D5, and Wythoffians of reducible groups are prisms/duoprisms already covered; the 45 polychoral prisms, the grand antiprism prism and the duoprism prisms {p}×{q}×{ } are all prisms over convex uniform 4-polytopes; the duoprismatic families {q,r}×{p} are polyhedron × polygon. This sidesteps the counting subtleties (B5/D5 duplicates, {4}×{4}×{ } = 5-cube).

Taking ALL convex uniform polyhedra / 4-polytopes in the product cases includes antiprism × polygon and prisms over antiprismatic prisms. These are genuinely convex uniform 5-polytopes; the article's Coxeter-group families ([p]×[q]×[ ] etc.) contain them only implicitly via alternations. A literal reading excluding them would make the completeness statement false, so they are included. Reviewer should confirm this reading.

'Wythoffian' is formalized as the reflective Wythoff construction only (finite group generated by affine hyperplane reflections, via `EuclideanGeometry.reflection`). Uniform alternated forms in the article (D5 forms as B5 alternations, the snub 24-cell prism) are covered by the other cases (D5 is itself a reflection group; the snub 24-cell prism is a prism over a uniform 4-polytope). Nonuniform alternations (B4×A1 snubs) are excluded by the uniformity hypothesis.

Uniform polytope defined recursively on dimension d: d=0 point; d+1: polytope (convex hull of a finite set) of affine dimension d+1, vertex-transitive under affine isometries of the ambient space, all edges of equal length, all facets uniform d-polytopes. For d=2 this gives exactly the regular polygons (vertex-transitive convex polygon with equal edges), for d≥3 Wikipedia's definition; the edge-length condition is redundant for d≥3 but included as in the decomposition notes.

Faces are nonempty exposed subsets (`IsExposed ℝ P F`) of a given affine dimension `Module.finrank ℝ (vectorSpan ℝ F)`; all faces of a polytope are exposed. Vertices are `P.extremePoints ℝ`. Edge length is `Metric.diam`.

Cartesian products are encoded as Minkowski sums `A + B` with `A ⊆ U`, `B ⊆ Uᗮ` for a subspace `U`, which avoids `WithLp 2 (E × F)` and absorbs translations; a prism is the case of a segment factor (its length is forced to equal the edge length by the uniformity hypothesis).

No explicit 'up to similarity' quotient: each disjunct is invariant under similarities of ℝ^5, and the answer(sorry) variant asks for the full set of subsets of ℝ^5, which is closed under similarities.
Ambient space is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 5)` (notation `ℝ^5` from FormalConjecturesForMathlib); definitions are stated for a general finite-dimensional real inner product space.

Extra variant `uniform_5_polytope.variants.find : {P | IsUniformPolytope 5 P} = answer(sorry)` records the statement's literal 'find and classify the complete set' form; two `@[category test]` lemmas (a point is a uniform 0-polytope; a point is Wythoffian) are proved.

reviewer_notes: Ambiguities: (1) The source is an imperative ('find and classify'); the decomposition fixes the Prop as completeness of the known list. The final file states that Prop as the main theorem and records the literal open-ended form as `uniform_5_polytope.variants.find` with answer(sorry). (2) Membership of the infinite families: the article's Coxeter-family tables ([3,3]x[p], [4,3]x[p], [5,3]x[p], [p]x[q]x[ ]) are narrower than its prose ('Cartesian products of the uniform polyhedra and regular polygons'); the file uses the broad reading (products of ANY convex uniform polyhedron/4-polytope with a regular polygon/segment), which is the only reading under which the completeness claim is not trivially false (antiprism x polygon, snub cube x polygon, prisms over antiprismatic prisms are convex uniform 5-polytopes; the article includes them implicitly as alternations 'not shown'). All three formalizing candidates made this choice independently. (3) 'Wythoffian' is the reflective Wythoff construction (orbit polytope of a finite reflection group); uniform orbit polytopes are exactly the ringed-diagram Wythoffians (edges of an orbit polytope are x—s x for reflections s, so equal edges = equidistance from the active mirrors). Non-reflective known members (snub 24-cell prism, grand antiprism prism) fall under the prism clause. (4) The count 104 is not formalized as a cardinality; the classes are described structurally, which sidesteps the B5/D5 and {4}x{4}x{ } = 5-cube duplicate-counting subtleties. Verdict on bail-outs (c01, c04, c07, c08): their claim that explicit coordinates for all 104 sporadic polytopes are needed is not correct, since the known list is exactly characterised by similarity-invariant structural classes; their secondary objection (the article only says 'known', not 'conjectured complete') is addressed by also including the answer(sorry) variant.
